newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Foreign troops reach violence-stricken Albania.
newsitem.headline: Foreign troops reach violence-stricken Albania.

text.p: Italian, French and Spanish troops arrived by air and sea in Albania on Tuesday in a well-orchestrated show of military force to launch a multinational effort to safeguard humanitarian aid supplies.
A force of 1,200 began landing in the western port city of Durres and at Tirana airport shortly after dawn. A total of 6,000 are due to reach the volatile Balkan nation within the next three weeks.

Albania's Prime Minister Bashkim Fino warmly welcomed the arrival of U.N.-backed "Operation Alba". He said the presence of foreign soldiers would help restore peace and order to a country racked by months of lawlessness and violence.

"The government of Albania extends its best thanks in the name of the Albanian people for the readiness demonstrated in helping us at this delicate time," Fino said. "They will help Albania overcome the grave crisis that has gripped our country."
More than 300 people have died and 700 have been injured during the armed anarchy that swept Albania following the collapse of a string of fraudulent get-rich-quick savings schemes earlier this year.
Tens of thousands of weapons ended up in the hands of rebel gangs and ordinary Albanians after raids on armouries left undefended when soldiers and police deserted their posts.
There were still no signs on Tuesday of an end to the violence. Police killed an escaped convict in a shootout in the southeastern town of Bilisht after he had shot and wounded two police officers.
In the northern town of Shkoder, a gunman shot dead a hospital patient undergoing surgery for gunshot wounds.

Fino's emergency all-party government appealed in vain a month ago for foreign military intervention to help disarm the population. The multinational force that began arriving on Tuesday under Italian command will limit its operations to protecting aid convoys.
"We are here to help Albania in a moment of national difficulty," said Italian Defence Minister Beniamino Andreatta, who flew to Durres to observe the landing.
"I think all Albanians understand this," Andreatta said, adding that the main aim of Operation Alba was "to leave behind a country reunified with a renewed sense of national identity.

Just moments after six Italian military planes carrying 150 paratroopers landed at Tirana airport, the French troop transport ship Orage with 450 French soldiers reached Durres, Albania's main port 40 km (25 miles) west of the capital.
In cold, windy conditions, the French troops began unloading four helicopters, six tanks and dozens of armoured vehicols as the Italian navy flagship Vittorio Veneto patrolled offshore.
French general Maurice Godinot, deputy commander of the force, was welcomed in Durres by Mayor Arqili Gorea.
"The multinational force is here to bring security to Albania," Godinot said. "We are ready to bring assistance."
A team of 60 French marines had made a sweep of Durres harbour before the landing began because of reports there might be a guerrilla attack, French military officials said.

"We got information last night from the Italians that there were rumours of terrorist actions in Durres," a senior French official said. "Because we didn't take risks, we sent a sufficient number of commandos to secure the harbour."
The Italian amphibious assault ship San Marco dropped anchor next to the Orage and 200 Italian troops disembarked.
The Spanish ship Hernan Cortes with 350 Spanish troops on board followed the Orage into Durres.
Dozens of Albanians watched the disembarcation of troops and equipment. Many said the troops were a symbol of hope for Europe's poorest country.
"These troops are welcome in Albania," said Pjeter Jame, a teacher who travelled from Tirana to witness the landing. "Right now they are the only hope of the Albanian people."
The U.N. World Food Programme plans to distribute aid throughout Albania as soon as possible. A ship with 400 tonnes of wheat, beans and vegetable oil was due on Tuesday.
Officials said the country's poor were desperately in need of food and one in 10 Albanians needed humanitarian aid.
Admiral Guido Venturoni, Italy's defence chief of staff and overall commander of the eight-nation force, said the troops would use force if necessary to defend themselves.
He also said the soldiers would not stand by and do nothing if they witnessed violence against individuals, as U.N peacekeepers had to do in Bosnia at times.
Greece, Turkey, Austria, Denmark and Romania are also contributing soldiers to the mission.
